claims.quote: A change is followed through every relation goal of a rule, wherever it stands: in a `find`, in a goal used as a value, and in a rule's head, as well as in its body and under `not`. Counting with zeros, `["aggregate/count", ["find", "?id", ["order", "?id", "?c", "?_"]]]` in a head, no longer starts over at each change: with a million facts, adding a fact and asking every count takes 13 milliseconds, where it took 0.26 seconds.

An aggregate that recurses, such as shortest distances by `aggregate/min`, goes on from the rows it has when facts change. With 100,000 roads, adding a road and asking every distance takes 15 milliseconds, where it took 0.7 seconds.

A rule that invents is followed through a change where it invents alone into a relation with no key: with 100,000 facts, adding a fact and asking its rows takes 70 milliseconds, where it took a second. A relation that cannot be followed, one that rules invent rows of into a keyed relation or beside other rules, one whose rule holds a function from the host, or one whose rule reads a changed relation through a schema, is derived again and compared with what it was, once something has read it since the last change, so the relations that read it are followed instead of forgotten.

says.statement: A relation that cannot be followed through a change is derived again and compared with what it was, once something has read it since the last change, so the relations that read it are followed

claims.quote: A `rule` form keeps the rows of the relations whose rules did not change, a change an invariant refuses leaves what was derived in place, and a goal-directed query keeps what it derived and follows changes. With a million facts, asking every row of a rule after a fact was refused takes 0.23 seconds, where it took 2.7, and after a rule was added to another relation 0.24 seconds, where it took 1.9.
`bun run mutate` breaks copies of the working tree under `out/metrics/`, as it stood when the run began, four at a time, so the code can be edited while it runs. `--jobs` says how many run at once.
